title: Atomic Structure and Isotopes
seo_title: Atomic Structure Worksheets: Protons, Neutrons, Electrons and Isotopes (High School Chemistry)
standard_text: Use the periodic table as a model to predict the relative properties of elements based on the patterns of electrons in the outermost energy level of atoms.
meta_desc: Free high school chemistry worksheets on atomic structure (NGSS HS-PS1-1): protons, neutrons and electrons, isotopes, average atomic mass, ions and electron shells. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Neutrons make isotopes; outer electrons decide how an atom reacts.
body_html:
How to think about it

Protons decide the element; electrons decide how it reacts.

  • Atomic number = protons. Mass number = protons + neutrons. Neutral atom: electrons = protons.
  • Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons. Average atomic mass is weighted by how common each isotope is.
  • Electrons fill shells 2, 8, 8, … The outer (valence) electrons control chemistry. Ions gain or lose electrons.
Example

Neutrons in sodium-23 (atomic number 11)?

23 − 11

Answer: 12

Example

Electrons in O2− (8 protons)?

Gain 2 electrons: 8 + 2

Answer: 10

Common mistakes

  • Using the mass number as the number of neutrons.
  • Thinking an ion changes its number of protons.
  • Taking a simple average of isotope masses.

faq.q: How do you find the number of neutrons?
faq.a: Subtract the atomic number from the mass number. For carbon-14: 14 − 6 = 8 neutrons.

faq.q: What is the difference between isotopes and ions?
faq.a: Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons. Ions have gained or lost electrons and carry a charge.

faq.q: How is average atomic mass calculated?
faq.a: Multiply each isotope's mass by its fraction (percent ÷ 100) and add the results.
